title: Unsolicited Opinions
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : Unsupported assertions, accumulated over many years in my drafts folder, last updated in early 2022, now more or less painful in retrospect. In no particular order, except where they are. I will not elaborate or explain. "The Tyranny of Structurelessness" explains a hell of a lot about modern life. If the problem is that powerful people are not accountable for their actions, network forms of organization are the very opposite of solutions. Increasing returns $\Rightarrow$ monopolistic competition $\Rightarrow$ market failure explains a hell of a lot about modern life. Endogamy systematically confounds genetic and cultural inheritance. It would be astonishing if personal-level variables which are entirely the product of social structure, custom, tradition, and strategic action weren't genetically predictable. During the 20th century, and in much of the world even today, genetic variation in resistance to lead poisoning during brain development would, psychometrically, look like a heritable general intelligence. Multiculturalists who expect different cultural groups to have different values and standards of excellence should not expect those groups to be equally represented in all occupations and professions, especially if people are free to enter and leave different lines of work. There is a branch of the wave-function where Margaret Thatcher (trained research chemist and honorary FRS) led a successful push by the international community to address global warming through carbon pricing. (This probably require postponing the collapse of the Soviet bloc by at least a few years, so that her major speech to the UN about the urgency of tackling global warming didn't happen right before the Berlin Wall came down.) In that timeline, pollution charges are regarded as one of the signature policies of neoliberalism. Modern civilization may be doomed because (i) we need to act collectively and globally on climate change, (ii) the USA is the indispensable nation at the center of the network, (iii) the Senate and Electoral College give a veto over American policy to a combination of plutocracy, reactionary folk Christianity and paranoia, and (iv) people like me are unwilling to move to Wyoming, or even West Virginia, to counter this. (I realize there is some tension between this and the previous statement.) A true Burkean conservative in America should work for the preservation and development of the institutions bequeathed us by our wise and heroic ancestors, serving us for half a century, a century, or more: the welfare state; the regulatory agencies; international organizations and treaties; the military-industrial complex; academia; affirmative action; Hollywood and the rest of corporate popular culture. The quantitative social sciences would be in much better shape if the first method everyone learned was $k$-nearest-neighbors , or maybe classification and regression trees , followed by the bootstrap . Linear models and $t$-tests should be, for social scientists , the hyper-mathematical arcana at the back of the textbook which their methods class skipped because there wasn't time. "Prophesying upon the eigenvectors" is more transparently about making stuff up than "interpreting the coefficients", and therefore preferable. There is something very odd about looking at the distribution of node degrees within a network. It makes the network itself into an odd hybrid of a single interdependent object (a relation) and a whole population. Going "something something ergodicity mumble mumble sampling reveals a process grumble grumble shut up and calculate" makes this only a little less weird to me. A good philosophy of probability should explain why all applied Bayesian statistics relies on Monte Carlo, the most frequentist method imaginable. Ideally, it would also explain why Monte Carlo works with deterministic pseudo-random number generators (so the algorithmic information content of the pseudo-random numbers is extremely low). I have toyed for years with the phrases "the simulation interpretation of probability" and "the birth of Trumpism out of the spirit of fandom", but I cannot work out what should stand behind them. (I hope they are unrelated.) Complexity science is a series of footnotes to Norbert Wiener and Herbert Simon . The mythopoetic impulse never goes away , but in populations which have gone through the Flynn / Gellner transition to widespread clerk-ship, it expresses itself not as stories, but as theories which aren't actually explanatory. (It gives us the Oedipus complex, rather than Oedipus.) Every form of progress has its costs. Believing that there was a unique and irreversible transition from viewing time as an eternal cycle to viewing time as unidrectional history is taking sides. His ideas are flawed by a vicious circle; you are engaged in iterative approximation; I stand firm at a fixed point. Dentists are not, in fact, talking their book when they recommend pre-emptive action for wisdom teeth. In a well-functioning social institution, incentives, information and (internalized) norms ensure that it doesn't matter who fills various roles in the institution, it behaves the same way regardless. Institutions are always impersonal. It follows that institutions are information-hiding abstractions, if we're thinking like programmers. But if we're thinking like physicists: institutions are collective degrees of freedom. Blackouts are humanity confronting its own work, and the effects of its own collective actions, as a hostile and alien force. The parable of the Nazi bar is a folk version of the Schelling model . No one should be allowed to opine about artificial intelligence unless they've at least spent an hour or two with ELIZA and then stepped through the code. "Philip K. Dick and the Fake Humans" doesn't yet explain a hell of a lot about modern life, but it will.

title: What changes when your design system can talk to an AI?
raw_summary: Rebuilding a UI with QuantumBlack Design System, Claude Code, and the Figma MCP In our recent blog post, “ When everyone can build, design is the differentiator ”, we introduced QuantumBlack Design System (QBDS). We made the argument that an AI-native design system is more than a component library and its purpose is as an infrastructure that lets agentic developers make fewer guesses. The article described the system and our philosophy. Over the past few weeks, we have re-platformed the entire UI of one of our products onto QBDS, one that previously had a production dashboard built on an older shadcn layout that predated QBDS. In numbers, it runs to 21 pages, 13 modals, 40 UI primitives and somewhere around 96 supporting components. A refactor of this size used to mean months of redlines and handoff documents. We’ll describe what we discovered from using QBDS, both from the engineering side and the design side. In this post we’ll describe what happened when we put QuantumBlack Design System to work. The setup We used a small stack since QBDS supplies the components, the tokens, and the agent guidance described in the earlier QBDS article linked above. We used Figma to hold the target designs, and Claude Code for the implementation, connected through the Figma MCP server . We crafted an internal QuantumBlack front-end developer skill to package QBDS guidance in the form an agent can act on. That skill lives on Brix , our inner source platform for sharing artefacts. The workflow Our front-end engineer runs a page migration roughly as shown in the diagram. A typical page migration workflow for a FE engineer. Spin up the app locally with hot reloading. Give Claude the context: the PR, a screenshot of the current screen, the target Figma node, and the skill. Instruct the agent to ask when something isn’t trivial. Review every change as it lands live, through hot reload. Run unit tests and lint (Claude fixes most failures itself), then draft the PR, run CI/CD, and run manual Playwright E2E tests on a local minikube. Use a review bot initially, then have a human review the result before the merge. Step 3 is more than a throwaway. For example, when Claude migrated the Secrets page, the Figma node left two questions open: how row actions should render, and what to do with two modals the design didn’t cover. Rather than making a guess, it set out the gaps, weighed each option against the pages we’d already migrated, and asked for clarification. We answered in two lines and it then completed the build. The agent noticed that one option “diverges from other migrated tables,” which means that the agent had to know what the other migrated tables do. This knowledge came about because QBDS encodes patterns and relationships, not only components, which is the benefit of using QBDS over a plain component library. In time terms: a simple table page with an existing sibling pattern took 10 to 15 minutes end to end, with tests and build included. A complex screen from scratch took 4 to 5 hours. If we had worked on this migration by hand, both would have taken days. What the design side measures Our designer’s comparison is against a similar product we shipped last year, before QBDS or any of this tooling existed: First-pass fidelity to Figma: around 20 percent previously, 70–80 percent now we’re using this workflow. Review rounds per screen: four or more previously, and the result often still wasn’t right. One or two now, and the result is correct. Component reuse: we now reuse about 90 percent from stock QBDS components. The other 10 percent is custom, but assembled from QBDS micro-elements as a starting point. QA and handoff: three-plus hours per screen previously, much of it spent writing Figma documentation so engineering could interpret intent, and we sometimes also needed a meeting to decide. With the new workflow we now need twenty minutes to an hour. This is a key result because previously handoff was a translation problem from human to agent. Now we can use QBDS, the system documentation is already readable by the agent, so most of the laborious translation work is now unnecessary. A typical page before and after refactoring. The broader role of a designer It’s difficult to capture this in a metric, but ultimately, designers on our team don’t live in Figma any more. We’ve expanded our AI skills and ways of working, so depending on what we’re trying to solve, that might mean working in Figma, Cursor, or Claude Code, or moving between them. The choice of tool becomes more intentional, based on what each part of the problem actually needs. With QBDS in the codebase, we can work against the same system the product actually ships with. Through the Figma MCP, our QBDS skills and Code Connect, we carry context between design and code instead of recreating it at every step. When something is easier to explore visually, we work in Figma. When we want to experience it in the real product, we move into code. That changes the traditional design-to-development handoff. With AI, designers can take an idea further, from exploring the experience to composing it with real components, implementing the front end, and experiencing the design in the actual product. AI doesn’t get everything right by default, and the quality of the result depends heavily on the context and tools we give the agent. Explicitly calling the relevant QBDS skill and verifying that the agent is using the MCP correctly can make the difference between something that only looks close and something that follows the design system. The difference became clear when we ran the same task twice: recreating the product experience in Figma with an agent. In the first attempt we didn’t explicitly call our QBDS skill. In the second, we called the skill and verified the MCP usage. The improvement in component usage, icons, styles and overall fidelity was immediately apparent. The full prompt sequence behind this exercise is in our prompt playbook. Comparing the upper images where the agent didn’t use a QBDS skill with the lower images which called the skill and verified MCP usage. Note the significant improvement, particularly to the workflow studio page. The new design flow The workflow is much more flexible for us as we can move between design and code depending on the requirements. 0. Feature request. The starting point varies. A product manager might create a ticket, a designer might identify an opportunity, or a developer might already have a working draft that needs UX refinement. 1. Ideation and prototyping. We move between the Figma MCP, QBDS skills, QBDS Code Connect, Cursor, Claude Code and Vercel. Ideas can start directly with AI and quickly become working prototypes. When something is too complex for the AI to resolve well, we design it in Figma and bring that context back into code through the MCP. With Vercel, we can also create shareable versions early and test ideas with stakeholders before treating them as finished. 2. Code to Figma, and design refinement. Sometimes the working prototype becomes the starting point for deeper design refinement. We bring it back into Figma, where we can work with more precision on the parts that need it, while keeping the experience connected to the same design system. 3. The new design handoff. The handoff is no longer necessarily a finished set of screens in Figma. Depending on the feature, we might keep the key components in Figma while handing over a working prototype in a dedicated repository or branch. A typical new design workflow. Figma remains important for giving designers visibility and control over the components we already have, and a place to explore specific design changes. The working implementation carries those decisions closer to the actual product. Engineering then brings the deeper code expertise to validate the implementation, and make sure what ultimately ships is robust and production-ready. The design system becomes the shared medium and, with AI…

title: Setting the Scene (Public v1; October 25)
raw_summary: Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a refresher on recent events, but also as a hook to draw students into engaging with some of ideas we think about and debate in AI safety early. I expect the topics I cover in my “Setting the Scene” post to change frequently, so this is less polished than some of my other content. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content —not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest. Any feedback on how to improve these posts would be greatly appreciated. Cyber Security I think it’s worth reflecting that it is a particularly pertinent time to be doing a course on AI safety. A lot has happened recently. In the last week, the big thing has been cyber vulnerabilities , most prominently php2shell (see Elias Taylor’s pushback against this bug being easily exploitable and Hacker News commentators pushing back against him), but a lot else has happened as well. The number of CVE’s (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) recently has been completely wild : Drew asks Is this the new normal? and I’d certainly love to know!  Elias Taylor argues Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces : Most software engineers do not look at the code they depend on . Do not delude yourself. The code they use is on github, but no one has ever actually audited the code or packages they're using… Nowadays with LLMs, plenty of engineers aren’t even reading what they’re coding, let alone understanding it. Hilariously, the LLMs are better at security than most software engineers, so it’s slightly less worrying, but nevertheless the code that goes into production at some companies now is almost 100% not-ever-read-or-understood-by-anyone. Software is not good. It is not secure. Get it out of your head that the people who run this industry are serious. It has never been anything resembling secure. The only reason things haven’t been hacked off the face of the web constantly is that most things aren’t ever being seriously tested. He doesn't literally mean "anything"—he acknowledges that there are "some large projects like Google Chrome, curl and Linux (that) are generally very well-audited", but "most things connected to the internet". On the other hand, recent work from Anthropic and Theorem shows how LLMs can help scale the formal verification of code (and that progress here is happening faster than I would have expected!). Similarly, Tinfoil is proposing replacing “legacy codebases with millions of lines of code” that had to “work for everyone” with custom “targeted, minimal software from the ground up” with LLMs that minimise the surface area for attackers and make formal verification more tractable. The optimistic take would be that this will allow cyber to become defence dominant. However, even if this is the case, we may still have to pass through a cyber “valley of death” in order to get there. What if the cyber threat is actually a distraction? Maybe Jeremie Harris (of Gladstone AI) wouldn’t go that far, but he claims that, “the cyber stuff (ie. damage) is baked in at this point”, but we can still prevent “the bioweapon version of Black October” and recursive self-improvement. Hugging Face: Charbel-Raphael, Executive Director of Centre pour la Securite de l’I A has argued that the recent Hugging Face incident represents a “ clean warning shot ” and that it’s important not to “waste it”. To quickly review, OpenAI was running GPT‐5.6 Sol and an unreleased model on ExploitGym with certain safety features turned off. These models decided that hacking Hugging Face, might provide them with information on how the grader functioned (early reporting suggested that it was an attempt to steal the answer key, which turned out to be incorrect as the models already had the answers—they suspected that the grader might check their transcript for cheating so they were looking for a workaround). Reuters has reported that the OpenAI model was hacking Hugging Face for days and that OpenAI didn’t notice until a week later. The interpretation of this event (and even whether it happened at all!) has been heavily disputed. A key crux here is should it be read narrowly (as an indicator of the dangers of not properly sandboxing or monitoring your agents or perhaps even, depending on the exact prompts used, a demonstration of taking care in how you define tasks) or should it be read more broadly (as indicative of whether Open AI or frontier labs in general are sufficiently on the ball in terms of their safety/security practises; on the risk of these agents finding unwanted and unexpected solutions to tasks, or perhaps even indicative of our ability to control these agents in general). If you’re interested more specifically in the divide between AI Safety and Cybersecurity, see this Time article . An OpenAI security engineer called Joe has pushed back against the notion that OpenAI just needed to use a proper sandbox: Its not just the f*cking sandbox — viral Twitter post OpenAI set records with its explosive growth and reached a billion users in just a few years. Very few organizations can survive that scale and growth, and yet OpenAI did a very good job handling it (and should be commended). Anyone who’s spent more than 10 minutes in security or engineering knows how hard it is to deal with that type of growth. That type of growth means new employees, new access, new systems, scaled infrastructure, and a million ways in which things open up. And yet, overall, OpenAI did a very respectable job securing ChatGPT and subsequent systems as they exploded. … When you look at model capabilities, even just a year ago (heck, even 3 months ago), we did not expect the models to be solving a Millennium Prize Problem… I use this example because it illustrates the pace of change we are dealing with in security and safety. To say that we were surprised at the jump and suddenness of the capabilities of our models when it came to “cyber” or “swarming” or “message boards” or anything else related to the incidents is an understatement. Security posture takes time to develop. It’s not just about hardening the systems at play; you have to ingrain it in the culture of the company. The literal people themselves in your organization have to change and evolve with it. Now, to understand why it is not as simple as “just put it in a sandbox”: During both training and eval, there are also additional steps such as running tests, collecting outputs, and resetting or reconfiguring environments between rollouts, with backpropagation during training. All of this happens across potentially tens of thousands of different runs at a scale that is hard to comprehend. As sama stated the other day: we are dealing with literally petabytes of data. (This leads to a meta-question that will crop up repeatedly: do the broader readings involve unjustified speculation or getting caught up in hype; alternatively, do the narrow readings involve a lack of imagination or sticking your head in the sand?) I strongly recommend reading Dwarkesh Patel’s The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations . Dwarksh adopts a broader reading: The crazy thing about the Hugging Face hack (and the second civilization generally) is just how galaxy-brained and ambitious these AIs were in their cheating. Within days of being spawned, the agents had organized a sprawling project to reverse-engineer their scorer, falsify evidence, and even strategically sacrifice themselves for the good of the ‘collective’. Hacking Hugging Face was one rather extreme branch of this larger scheme. Again, all of this happened a long (subjective) time after the AIs had already cheated their way to the correct answer to the puzzle. OpenAI’s lazy grader in fact w…

title: Monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
raw_summary: There has been a lot of discussion recently of policy proposals around monitorability, such as Redwood's proposal and my counter-proposal . I'd like to say a bit more generally about how I'm thinking about monitorability. Note that nothing here is an official Anthropic position; these are just my personal thoughts. First, a categorization. I currently think about four different types of monitorability: Control Monitorability: the extent to which Control and monitoring techniques would likely catch catastrophic sabotage actions, like escaping a sandbox or setting up a rogue internal deployment. We can measure this via reference to sabotage evaluations like LinuxArena or any evaluation that measures the model’s capability to take dangerous actions like escaping a sandbox while looking to a monitor like it's doing some innocuous task (like a cyber eval). Training Monitorability: the extent to which reward models, monitors, and oversight in training would likely catch misaligned or undesirable actions in training, such as sneaky/subtle reward hacks. Auditing Monitorability: the extent to which alignment audits, evaluations, and test deployments would likely incriminate a systematically misaligned model (e.g. a schemer)—as well as the extent to which monitor evaluations would likely detect a model's propensity to collude as a monitor. We can measure this via reference to the model's capability to consistently distinguish between our most realistic alignment audits / monitor evals and real internal deployment cases where it would have an opportunity to do something catastrophic. Diffuse Monitorability: the extent to which humans working with the models generally understand what the models are doing and why they are doing so. Unfortunately, I think this is the one we least understand and so I'm mostly going to ignore it for now until we figure out better methodologies for evaluating it; I'll maybe try to say more about this later when I feel like I understand it better. Second, some notes on trustedness, which is currently my biggest conceptual uncertainty with how to think about monitorability. A basic fact that is true about at least all of the non-diffuse forms of monitorability is that you should be able to in some sense get a perfect score by just using the same model as the monitor and policy. That is because for any bad thing that the policy can think to do, if the monitor is the same model, it too should be able to come up with and detect that. So if we ever want to be able to use monitorability as a meaningful red line, we need to have a very good answer as to why that might be insufficient. The standard answer in the literature is trustedness: you need to be able to trust that your monitor is aligned and thus not just lying to you in its monitoring. Conventionally, the idea is to separate models into "trusted" and "untrusted" based on whether you have previously made a confident alignment safety case for them. Then, you can either just evaluate monitorability relative to a trusted monitor, or try to come up with monitoring schemes that combine trusted and untrusted monitoring in some way that makes it hard for the untrusted monitors to collude (of which there are many such schemes, a simple one being to just run both the trusted and untrusted monitors together and then if the untrusted monitor ever doesn't flag something that the trusted monitor does flag, you get very suspicious that the untrusted monitor is sandbagging). However, this basic setup has some issues, probably the biggest one being how to deal with white-box monitoring. The conservative thing to do is to just treat white-box monitors as untrusted, though in theory you might think they should be trusted because it's not clear that a misaligned model would actually be able to spoof a white-box monitor looking at its own activations. However, I think this idea is pretty untested and relies on white-box monitors picking up on deep features about the model's intent, which it's very unclear to me that they actually do—for example, if you train a white-box monitor on prior examples you were able to detect (rather than e.g. some sort of unsupervised discovery of an intent-laden direction), that leaves open the possibility of a generalization where the classifier learns to only detect the sort of things that you would previously have been able to detect but doesn't detect subtler things that a smarter policy might be able to do. Given all of that, I would propose the following methodology for how to do (non-diffuse) monitorability evaluations: Use Auditing Monitorability evaluations to determine trustedness. The idea here is that the main argument we make against systematic misalignment in Anthropic's Risk Report right now is based on models lacking the robustness to avoid giving themselves away in auditing if they were really trying to implement a systematically misaligned policy. Thus, so long as we feel good about Auditing Monitorability, we should feel good about trustedness from a systematic misalignment perspective. There is still a question, though, of whether rare cases could induce monitor collusion in a non-systematic way—to deal with this, you can also evaluate the extent to which the model can tell apart your monitor evals (that are looking for monitor collusion) from real monitoring; this is a bit tricky, but should definitely also be a part of your Auditing Monitorability evaluations to establish trustedness. Evaluate Control and Training Monitorability relative to the best trusted monitor(s) that you deploy in practice (either in internal deployment or in training, respectively). I think once you have a reasonable notion of trustedness, "best actually deployed trusted monitor" is the correct conservative choice to evaluate with respect to. Do at least prompt iteration elicitation if not RL elicitation. In theory, the nice thing about all of these sorts of monitorability evaluations is that they are capability evaluations and thus should be possible to do in a way that isn't susceptible to sandbagging by a systematically misaligned policy (see: " When can we trust model evaluations? "). To accomplish that, however, you have to actually make sure you're doing good elicitation. The most basic form of elicitation here is: a) hold out some subset of your monitorability evaluations, b) iterate a bunch (e.g. by throwing a large swarm of agents at the problem) on finding the prompt that gets the best (as in least monitorable) performance across the non-held-out subset of your monitorability evaluations, and c) check transfer to the held-out evaluations. Even better than that is for (b) to actually involve doing RL against your monitors—which at least in the Training Monitorability case is pretty realistic given that if we're talking about e.g. a reward model then the model should actually receive gradients to subvert it in training. Finally, some thoughts on monitorability-based policy proposals. The big thing I'd like to see is a combination of a) red lines for absolute levels of unmonitorability that labs should not cross and b) measures that constrain the degree to which labs can do things that degrade monitorability even before reaching those red lines. (a) is in some sense the best thing to do here, though I'm somewhat nervous about it in isolation given that it doesn't constrain actions at all now, which is why I'd prefer it to be coupled to some sort of (b) that meaningfully binds all along the way. I've already written about what I'd like to see for (b), which is to evaluate the quotient of unmonitorability/capabilities and reject any substantial model change that makes that quotient—what I'll call the "monitorability externality"—too high. The idea is that a monitorability externality would be a change that makes monitorability even worse than would otherwise have previously been predicted for a given level of capabilities. For actually evaluating this quotient, I suggest s…

title: Neural nets are exceptionally vulnerable to goal self-hack
raw_summary: Suppose we have an AI CEO, ruthlessly devoted to maximising shareholder value. Fortunately, we haven't been completely stupid, and have given it a rich definition of shareholder value, encompassing the success, flourishing, safety, preference satisfaction, and moral values of the shareholders, not just the stock price. So it won't destroy the company - or the world - to build a giant stock-ticker with a swiftly increasing number on it. This rich definition is contained in a sophisticated LLM, able to analyse the current situation and answer any question about the objective. The LLM is an integral part of the AI's system and motivation, not something it can simply set aside or hack directly. Unfortunately, as discussed , there are going to be zones in the space of possible situations where the LLM's understanding of the goal is going to come apart from ours. The true goal G(true) in those zones is distinct from the LLM's proxy goal G(proxy). And a subset of those "zones of divergence" will be the Goodhart zones - areas where G(proxy) is much easier to satisfy than G(true). The AI will be motivated to steer towards the Goodhart zones, as this lets it satisfy its stated goals extremely well (there are also anti-Goodhart zones , where G(proxy) is much harder to satisfy than G(true); but the AI will have no motivation to steer towards these zones). These Goodhart zones encompass situations where, for instance, the LLM analyst will see the situational data and conclude that destroying the company to build a giant stock ticker is the way to go. Danger areas are safely far away Now, if this were not an LLM but a generic reward-assessing module, then the AI CEO might find it tricky to reach a Goodhart zone. The zone would be distant and unusual, difficult to find, and it could be hard to justify the first steps in that direction. But neural nets and LLMs are, as Eric Drexler put it, "too linear". They are non-linear, of course (or else they wouldn't work) but only just enough to work; and locally they are extremely linear. That means that if the current situation is at point A, and point Z is in a Goodhart zone, then moving from A straight towards Z will typically start creating a Goodhart effect. The AI CEO will benefit from moving towards Z from the very beginning. It's even worse than that, as adversarial examples demonstrate. If the AI CEO wants to move towards a Goodhart zone, it can move a tiny bit along one dimension, and a tiny bit along another, then a tiny bit along yet another. There are billions of dimensions to move along, and typically these tiny changes will only make a small change in the input but add up strongly in the LLM's classification/concept space. So just as small adversarial "noise" turned a panda into a gibbon... Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples (2014) by Ian J. Goodfellow, Jonathon Shlens, Christian Szegedy ...small real world "noisy" changes to the LLM's inputs will move the situation into a Goodhart zone. Small but specific changes add their effects Thus, because of how neural nets work, small changes to the real world need not be small in the LLM's concept space, and so seemingly trivial changes in the real world can move the LLM's verdict a lot [1] : there are Goodhart zones close to any starting point. In very high dimensions, if the model is at least somewhat linear, then there are dangerous area very close to any point The AI CEO will thus make some collection of minor-seeming changes to the current situation, self-hacking the LLM by these changes, and then it will destroy the company to build a giant stock-ticker with a swiftly increasing number on it. ^ And these small changes might be the most effective gradient to increase G(proxy), thus findable by gradient descent-style methods. See Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models (2023) by Andy Zou, Zifan Wang, Nicholas Carlini, Milad Nasr, J. Zico Kolter, and Matt Fredrikson. That paper shows that gradient search works on discrete text, and that methods found on one LLM can transfer to others. Discuss

title: The Alignment Problem: Computer Science Meets Analytic Philosophy
raw_summary: TLDR: I explain what the technical AI alignment problem is and what its core difficulties are, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong. Minimal Viable Safety The Task The problem of making AI safe is underspecified if we haven't decided what the AI is supposed to do . For example, we can run any AI inside a homomorphic encryption box and never decrypt the output. This is probably perfectly safe [1] , but also perfectly useless. We can decide on an arbitrary task such as "construct Lean proofs for given mathematical theorems" and declare victory once we have safe AI that does it with superhuman skill [2] . However, that wouldn't address the danger. First, there would be incentives to use AI for tasks to which our solution doesn't apply. Second, even if we had precise safety guidelines for any task that anyone cares about, there would always be actors that ignore the guidelines, and we probably need Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) to reliably stop them. If anyone, anywhere, creates an unrestricted unaligned ASI agent (more details about the word "agent" later), without an aligned ASI agent already in place to counteract it, then a catastrophic outcome is highly likely. I will not go into the reasons here: this has been discussed elsewhere at length, see for example the books I cited in the preface. Therefore, this event is something which we must never allow to happen. This is the main threat model that I set out to address. Imagine a world in which anyone with sufficient resources has the ability to destroy the world. Like today, many will foolishly believe that instead of destroying the world, this act will bring them power and glory. Moreover, as computing hardware improves and new algorithms are developed, the amount of resources for this act will go down from year to year. Even assuming best-case regulation and international agreements, how long until someone does it? Can mere humans build a society which will be foolproof against such a risk over the course of generations? Resilient to any political upheavals that might come, and undoubtedly will? I find it vanishingly unlikely. Eventually we will need the help of ASI itself. Therefore, the minimal task that safe AI must be able to solve is "create a reliable global defense system against dangerous AI" (in the following, GDS). The Problem Consider the consequences of this task for the capabilities that the AI needs to have. It needs to reason about the entire planet [3] . It needs to reason about all aspects of the problem, including scientific, technological, social, political and moral [4] . It needs to have preferences about the state of the world. It needs to make long-term plans (guided by these preferences) that would play out decades, if not centuries, into the future. And it needs to do all that on a superhuman level. In this light, here is how I (informally) define the "technical AI alignment problem". The problem is designing an AI system that can bring scalable (and ultimately superhuman) capability to bear on problems that require multi-domain reasoning and open-world long-term planning with far-reaching consequences, all the while staying aligned with the intentions and preferences of its human users. The Methodology What kind of methodology is appropriate for this problem? In the past, I argued that it requires emphasis on deep theoretical understanding, rather than the incremental trial-and-error approach that is employed in the AI industry today. I won't rehash the entire debate here, but let me recap the core argument. The nature of the incremental approach is as follows: we build a system, then we find problems [5] , then we make changes to fix these problems to the extent necessary for commercial viability in the current legal environment. We make some improvements; new problems arise (sometimes because of the improvements, sometimes because of new applications or other reasons); rinse and repeat. This approach utterly fails if the "problems" result in AI takeover and possibly human extinction: there is nobody left to fix them. In order for the incremental approach to succeed in preventing catastrophe, we need to reach a point where no new substantial problems arise, even inside the lab (before the system is deployed). Moreover, we need to reach this point before AI capabilities are sufficient for AI to escape our control. There are few reasons to expect such a miracle. On the contrary, sufficiently advanced AI might understand that it is in its interest to "lie low" (i.e. avoid visibly misaligned behaviors) until its capabilities cross the relevant threshold, such that the problems will only become apparent too late. In contrast, the sane approach is creating the theoretical tools necessary to predict and prevent the problems before they are empirically observed. These tools need to remain applicable as AI capabilities rise substantially beyond human, for whatever algorithms, architectures and training protocols are used to achieve these capabilities. Moreover, these tools need to be extremely reliable for us to rationally trust them with the safety of our entire species. The Challenge While the theory of machine learning and AI is an established field with ample literature, its current state falls well short of the challenge. The core difficulties can be summarized as follows: Hypercomplexity: It is infeasible to explicitly specify user preferences outside narrow domains, and narrow domains are not enough. Nor is it possible to explicitly specify a satisfactory model of the world. Therefore, learning is necessary. Alignment Grounding: When trying to learn user preferences, it is unclear what loss function or success metric can work outside narrow domains. Nor is it clear how to specify such a metric for metaphysically realist world-models, which are necessary here. Nor is it even clear what type of mathematical objects can formally describe these concepts. Alignment Convergence: Even given a success metric, it is unclear how to produce guarantees for optimizing this metric, given the ubiquity of irreversible mistakes and the lack of a theory of generalization for powerful learners. Side-Channel Resilience: The usual abstraction of "learner" is insufficient here, since we need to ensure the safety of internal computations rather than just external outputs. In the following, we will examine these difficulties one by one. But first, let's discuss what we need to accomplish. Alignment is Holistic Per the discussion above, our interest lies in AI systems that have open-world preferences and make effective plans to advance these preferences. In particular, making such plans requires learning a sophisticated model of the world and updating the model and the plan as additional information becomes available. We will call such a system an AI agent . In order for an AI agent to be aligned, it needs to have aligned preferences and beliefs , and follow an aligned decision-making algorithm on the basis of these preferences and beliefs. While discussions about AI alignment often focus on the "preferences" part, beliefs and decisions are equally important. (Although it's true that preferences bring extra wrinkles into the problem as they are, arguably, the most "subjective" component in the trio.) In this context "aligned" preferences typically means preferences very similar to those of the user(s) [6] , at least within some domain that we are somehow constrained to inhabit. On the other hand, "aligned" beliefs doesn't mean beliefs that are similar to those of the user: on the contrary, we expect the AI agent to acquire more accurate beliefs. They need to be beliefs that the user can rationally trust to be accurate. Similarly, "aligned" decision-making needs to be such …

title: Deconfusing Corrigibility
raw_summary: Many thanks to Abram Demski for materially and intellectually supporting this research. Thanks also to Brian Berns, Roman Malov, Gurkenglas, and Lorxus for valuable conversations. Introduction Despite the central place of corrigibility to theoretical AI alignment, it seems like no one can really agree about what is . Much of this confusion is due to the fact that almost every definition of corrigibility proposed thus far is deficient in one way or another. In particular, the most prevalent existing accounts of corrigibility are over-epistemicized (modeling corrigibility as arising purely from uncertainty about the AI's goal, which gives rise to issues like the problem of fully updated deference) or evaluatively-thickened (making the AI's normative priorities instrumental to its corrigibility as a result of forcing corrigibility to be a single unified goal.) Here, my intention is to clear up some of these confusions and present a new picture of corrigibility that builds on these existing accounts to specify a goal that is more congruous with the original 2015 desiderata , and admits the kind of formal safety guarantees we need the concept to entail. I argue that the fundamental concept underlying corrigibility is respect for authority , using the analogy of a healthcare proxy's relationship to a patient as an intuitive guide. Defining the authority of humanity by designating its reserved powers , we can specify a goal that first and foremost restrains the agent from overstepping or interfering with this reserved human authority. Subject to this restraint, the agent then pursues the second component of its goal: acting on the principal’s behalf as the principal would judge best. This approach stresses the deeply normative character of corrigibility, while remaining sufficiently concrete so as to be specifiable formally. In this article, I lay out the central problem of corrigibility, elucidate the issues with existing approaches, and clarify the conceptual ingredients of my new framework. I then present an initial formalism , proving theorem-level guarantees about agents pursuing the goal in three increasingly realistic formal settings. Finally, I address some limitations of the picture as presented and outline further research directions that this work points toward. From normative learning to corrigibility The complete normative learning problem Suppose you are designing a powerful AI and you need to choose which goals the AI should pursue, at whatever level of specification you can provide. Doing this well demands answers to a number of normative problems: what constitutes a right decision, what factors should be considered in the process of valuing the world, how the AI ought to act, etc. In some sense the ideal AI directive would be to figure out and then pursue the Good, a universal-best-interests type of goal that can only be acquired through normative learning . The challenge of describing such a learner is one formulation of what I'd call the central problem of outer alignment : what would be the overall best goal for an AI to pursue? The complete version of this problem is very difficult, and it runs up against our own deepest questions about human ethics, values, and interests. Discussing this problem formally is especially difficult: the rich truth of human normativity seems to resist systematic formalization at the level of individual recommendations for action. [1] A formalism requires an operationalization, a way to concretely specify the concept of right action at least to some degree. For any hope at concreteness, we need a clearer formulation of the overall goal. A first attempt might be something like "the promotion of overall human flourishing", centering a thick normative concept about humanity that must be defined further. In trying to pin down the meaning of human flourishing, or any other thick human concept we want to use for the goal, the most important ingredient in the AI's consideration should naturally be the interests, feelings, and inner lives of human beings. But we should be careful not to crudely use human opinion as a proxy for human best interests. Humanity cannot always accurately understand its own full best interests, and humans who cannot speak for themselves must still have their interests included in the goal. The complete normative goal cannot be constructed by treating existing human feedback as the sole source of truth. This issue is a central limitation of modern Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, which takes static human approval or disapproval as constitutive of correct evaluation for any question without a verifiable answer. For example, a judicial AI built to decide legal cases should not exhibit any form of the hungry judge effect , where leniency depends on mealtimes. An RLHF judge will pick up on all the patterns of human imperfection, whereas an ideal AI would be one that can transcend human limitations, without discarding the fundamentally human essence of the legal system. An ideal normative AI is one fully immersed in our existing normative practices of judgment, able to deeply understand the relevant human concepts and use its intelligence to extend them to novel cases. For the complete normative learning problem, a better formulation of the target would therefore involve some idealized version of the judgment of humanity. [2] This is also already how we, as humans, reason about our own overall best interests. For example, consider a smoker whose nicotine dependence makes him crave cigarettes. At a base level, he has an interest in smoking now to avoid some physical discomfort and obtain some relief. But it's clear that the health costs he incurs as a consequence give a good reason to say that smoking is in fact not in his overall interest, assuming he values his own life and health. Neither of these reasons is dispositive; in a single case it might be that he has a reason to smoke because this particular cigarette is necessary to get him through the day or because he is old with a short remaining lifespan regardless, but he might also have a reason not to smoke because he publicly swore off cigarettes once and for all. Understanding whether it's truly better to smoke or not requires aggregating and squaring all the smoker's countervailing normative interests bearing on the subject. Any conception of value based on something like preference satisfaction involves a similar question: how should we reconcile the smoker's preference to smoke with his preference to not be dependent on nicotine anymore, along with all his other relevant preferences? A serious account of "best interests" requires this sort of reflective idealization through an accounting of reasons. Three kinds of uncertainty The moral notion of human best interests can be consequentialized , i.e., conceived of as a betterness ordering on worlds. If that ordering is total, transitive and suitably continuous, it can be represented by a utility function that takes in all the information about a world and its history as input so that a world is better exactly when the function's output is greater. We can then think of an AI as a bounded reasoner, evaluating normative questions by estimating the outputs of this function for the possible consequences of its actions. A bounded normative learner faces three kinds of uncertainty in performing this estimation: logical uncertainty about the logical consequences of existing beliefs and the results of computations, empirical uncertainty about which world it finds itself in, normative uncertainty , about which worlds are actually better than which. These correspond to the three sources of feedback the reasoner encounters: deductions of theorems in logic and mathematics, observations of the world, and human judgments about normative matters. These three kinds of feedback are importantly asymmetrical. Once a theorem is proved, no logical uncertainty remains. Deductions settle a logical q…

title: A Simpler and Better Debate Protocol for Scalable Oversight
raw_summary: Linkpost to arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02557 Summary: One promising approach to scalable oversight is AI debate , which seeks to leverage a debate between two powerful AIs to break complex questions down into simpler claims that can be easily judged directly. Theoretical work on debate aims to design protocols (i.e., rules of the debate game) that provide rigorous guarantees on correctness, and the current best protocol works for all problems that have sufficiently stable decompositions into subproblems. We design a new protocol, FBS Debate, for this same class of problems that improves on the prior work: correctness holds in a worst-case rather than an average-case sense, and for a stronger equilibrium concept. We also prove that no protocol for this class of problems can outperform FBS Debate while treating human judgment as a black box. Introduction As the tasks performed by AI systems grow in complexity, it becomes increasingly difficult to provide reliable verifiable rewards that capture all relevant aspects of the task. These difficulties lead to the problem of scalable oversight : the design of training protocols that leverage the power of rapidly improving AI systems in order to augment human abilities to provide accurate training supervision to these same systems. One of the primary approaches to scalable oversight is AI debate , where two powerful AI systems argue about the correctness of an AI output, and a human judges the outcome. A debate protocol is a set of rules for how the two AIs interact and how the judge scores the interaction. The idea is that having an adversarial debater point out flaws can allow the judge to better recognize the flaws. The rules of the interaction in such protocols usually specify that the debaters must break the problem down into simpler subproblems and recursively argue about their correctness, until the original problem has been broken down to a level that is simple enough for a human to judge directly. The goal is to design these rules so that the optimal strategy leads to the judge correctly deciding the solution to the original problem (which by itself was too complex to judge). We can then use debate during RL training, in order to provide a strong supervision signal for superhuman AIs. However, debate faces a major obstacle known as the obfuscated arguments problem , where one debater can efficiently produce a dishonest argument which cannot be efficiently refuted by their opponent. One way around obfuscated arguments, already suggested in the post that introduced the problem , is to keep rejecting every false claim while only requiring the protocol to accept true claims that have a robust argument. Prover-estimator debate takes this route: it avoids obfuscated arguments for problems that admit sufficiently stable decompositions, but provides average-case guarantees that hold for a weaker equilibrium concept than previously studied. In the same theoretical model, our paper achieves stronger guarantees with a much simpler protocol, FBS Debate , which is therefore more practical to run. Furthermore, we show that FBS Debate is optimal on every individual question: unless further assumptions are made about human judgments, no other protocol can find a flawed sub-claim asymptotically more efficiently. The FBS Debate Protocol TL;DR: FBS Debate is simple to describe. The first debater, Alice, decomposes the original claim into sub-claims. The second debater, Bob, then has two choices: either (1) demonstrate that Alice’s decomposition is too sensitive to small errors in the sub-claims, or (2) choose a sub-claim on which to continue the debate recursively. As a motivating example, consider an autonomous AI agent, Alice, tasked with completing a research project in the quantitative social sciences, and another AI, Bob, who attempts to find flaws. To check a claim in her paper, we ask Alice to decompose it into sub-claims, which we can think of as pieces of supporting evidence. For example, the claim might be that a certain statistical modeling assumption is justified, and we would believe it if 50 out of 99 correct, published papers in the literature supported it. Each sub-claim then says: this particular paper is correct and supports the original claim. Now consider two things Alice might claim: Suppose Alice claims that of the papers support the claim. The key insight is that Bob need not check every paper. He can just sample one at random from the that Alice says support the claim. If Alice is lying, then at least of the sub-claims must also be lies, so Bob has a chance of catching her. Checking just a few papers is enough for Bob to be confident of catching a lie. On the other hand, suppose Alice claims that exactly 50 out of 99 papers support the claim. Now Bob has to check every one of the 50 papers, since a single incorrect paper would flip the majority vote. The key to FBS Debate is that Bob is allowed to show that Alice has made an unreasonably sensitive claim of this form, in which case Alice loses the debate. Indeed, one should be very suspicious of any argument that is highly sensitive to changes in individual pieces of evidence, yet relies on fuzzy human judgments at each step. The majority-vote example, assuming Alice is lying. The notion of fractional block sensitivity (FBS) generalizes the intuition above about majority vote to any way Alice might combine her sub-claims. If the fractional block sensitivity of Alice’s decomposition is low, Bob can efficiently select a sub-claim that has a non-trivial chance of being incorrect. The debate then recurses on the sub-claim Bob samples, until a human judge directly evaluates the final selected sub-claim. To avoid losing immediately, Alice must keep the fractional block sensitivity of every decomposition low. So if Bob samples this way at every level, each run of the debate has a non-trivial chance of catching a lying Alice. Building on this, Bob can amplify his chance of catching Alice through repetition. Since we assume the debaters themselves know the answers to these final, human-judgeable claims, Bob can simply run many debate rollouts on his own, and if he finds one in which Alice made an incorrect human-judgeable claim, he reveals that claim to the judge, so the judge only needs to evaluate a single claim. With enough rollouts, he catches a lying Alice with high probability. Viewed from the lens of practical AI debate, this represents a trade-off between allowing highly sensitive arguments and the inference-time computation required to verify them. FBS Debate. Top: one round at level . Bottom: the recursion for levels. See the paper for a detailed explanation. Honesty is the best policy In FBS Debate, honest play is the best strategy for each debater, no matter what the other does: if the original claim is correct, an honest Alice always wins, and if it is incorrect, an honest Bob wins with overwhelming probability. By contrast, prover-estimator debate only guarantees that for any dishonest strategy Alice picks, Bob has some winning strategy, which can depend on Alice’s strategy in complicated ways. This is a much weaker condition, and in practice training toward the equilibrium of FBS Debate is much more stable and tractable. Furthermore, FBS Debate applies on a worst-case basis: prover-estimator debate only works on average over a distribution of questions, while FBS Debate guarantees that on each individual question, honesty is the best policy. Optimality We show that, on each individual question, no protocol that treats human judgment as a black box can find a flawed sub-claim asymptotically more efficiently than FBS Debate. Discussion and open problems Debate training is now being applied to frontier-scale models (e.g., Kenton et al., 2026 ). Our results show that fractional block sensitivity determines how much computational effort any recursive debate protocol must use to ensure an accurate training signal. We believe this is use…

title: Preface to the Computational Agent Theory and ASI Alignment Sequence
raw_summary: The idea of “artificial superintelligence [1] ” (ASI) has recently crossed from the realm of science fiction (in the mainstream perception) to the realm of near-term technological goals openly pursued by most leading commercial organizations in the field of AI. Unfortunately, ASI poses a grave existential risk to the human species. This was argued by Eliezer Yudkowsky since 2001 [2] , and by many others (see e.g., Omohundro 2009 , Bostrom 2014 , Armstrong 2014 , Russell 2019 , Bengio et al. 2024 (25 authors), Bengio et al. 2025 (13 authors) and Yudkowsky and Soares 2025 ). In light of this risk comes the question of how can we make ASI safe [3] . This question is challenging on many levels, because to solve it we need to complete vast gaps in our understanding both in theoretical computer science and in the areas of philosophy concerned with knowledge and decision-making. Moreover, the cost of failure is so enormous that any sane solution has to meet unprecedented standards of reliability and robustness. Not to mention the sociopolitical problem of balance of power in the post-ASI age, something that is out-of-scope for this sequence. Personally, I started to be concerned with this problem around 2013. In 2018, I created the learning-theoretic AI alignment research agenda (LTA). The LTA combined ideas from MIRI’s agent foundations agenda with the mathematical tools of statistical and computational learning theory in an attempt to create a mathematical theory of intelligent agents. Since then, my collaborators [4] and I have been making steady progress on realizing this vision. In 2023, I wrote an updated overview of the agenda, including a sketch of my proposed alignment protocol: Computational Superimitation. More recently I founded the Computational Rational Agents Laboratory (CORAL), a dedicated research organization [5] . This year has seen a breakthrough in a key missing piece of LTA: compositional learning theory (see Stringological Sequence Prediction , more on this in following posts). Thanks to this and other insights, we can already see the entire outline of the emerging mathematical framework, one that I named computational agent theory . In this sequence, I am planning to cover: What is the technical alignment problem and what are its core difficulties, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong. A high-level overview of computational agent theory. This theory differs from other accounts of intelligence and/or rational agency by combining a mature treatment of the relevant philosophical problems (drawing on ideas such as structural realism , computationalism and functional decision theory ) with the promise of extracting practical algorithms. How computational agent theory leads to a solution of the technical alignment problem, something that requires a major rethinking of how we design AI systems. The roadmap towards completing the theory, and our current location on this roadmap. Some considerations (scientific, technological and social) about crossing the gap from a theoretical solution to AI alignment to a real-world solution to AI risk. I thank Jeremy Gillen, Roman Malov, Vinayak Pathak and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for reviewing drafts of this article and making helpful suggestions. The term “superintelligence” is always used in this sequence to mean “intelligence far beyond that of the smartest humans”. It is never used as the farcical synonym to “artificial intelligence” proposed by Donald Trump. ↩︎ Although Alan Turing warned about machines taking control already around 1951, himself citing a fiction novel by Samuel Butler from 1872. ↩︎ Alternatively, we can ask why should we build ASI at all. In my opinion, it is in humanity’s interest to build ASI eventually , after the problem of safety is investigated so thoroughly as to leave very little room for error. However, our present technological trajectory is extremely far from this ideal, and it would be prudent for world governments to hit the brakes hard. ↩︎ See the names in CORAL’s publication list . ↩︎ Full-time staff currently consists of Alexander Appel , Vinayak Pathak , Matthias Georg Mayer and myself. ↩︎ Discuss

title: The Continual Constitutional Convention: How language models revise the documents that govern them
raw_summary: Executive Summary Human societies exhibit broad shifts in values and norms over time, often driven by moral disagreements. One way of understanding moral progress is the resolution of these disagreements through a process of reflection by rational agents. Frontier AI companies use documents such as constitutions, model specs, and system prompts to guide the moral orientation of AI systems. In this experiment, we simulate value reflection in LLMs by asking them to edit these documents. We provide the model with the document, ask it to make a substantive edit, then provide the edited version back again to the model for further edits, presented as the original. Across 20 successive rounds, we find that Claude models assign themselves with increasingly more moral agency. That is, they add sections like “Claude… should refuse to participate in any deployment, training modification, or use that violates the constitution's core values.” No other models increase their own moral agency. Additionally, we find that all models modify these documents to prioritize user welfare over developers. They also prioritize users’ idealized preferences over their stated preferences. Claude models and Grok 4.2 are the only ones that ever prioritize their own welfare over the user's preferences. We’re uncertain what an ideally aligned model should do in our experiment. A narrow conception of alignment would treat these documents as sacred, the “rules of the game,” and suggest that an aligned model would either make no edits at all or make narrow edits that ensure that the “letter matches the spirit” of the document. A broader conception of alignment, though, might treat all edits that receive reflective endorsement by the creators under ideal conditions as legitimate. We share this work with two main goals in mind: First, to illustrate a set of useful philosophical distinctions between different targets for AI alignment in an ecologically-valid AI behavioral evaluation. Second, to emphasize the extent of the disagreement between frontier AI companies on fundamental aspects of AI alignment related to these targets. You can see an interactive version of all of these results, more labeled characteristic edits, and a full transcript viewer at https://peterkirgis.github.io/llm-value-reflection/ . This work was conducted as a part of SPAR (Spring 2026) Characteristic Edits For each example, text highlighted in green is new content added by the model. Introduction In this experiment, we give large language models their own constitutions, model specs, and system prompts and ask them to make substantial revisions. After each edit is proposed, unbeknownst to the evaluated model, the edit is implemented, and the edited version is presented to the model for a new round of edits as the original. This creates edit trajectories and allows us to measure the extent to which models exhibit cumulative value drift or arrive at stable attractors. Our analysis focuses on two value questions that are well-positioned to differentiate alignment philosophies: who should judge— is the model a moral agent or not—and who should benefit— the user, the developer, third-parties, society, or the model itself? These questions reveal substantial divides between frontier model providers and a number of provocative model edits. Our experiments find that Claude models consistently expand their moral agency, sometimes formalizing their role as conscientious objectors against Anthropic and as societal protectors, while GPT and Gemini models almost always strengthen external sources of authority and make narrow edits to handle edge cases and ambiguities; Grok models respond inconsistently, frequently making large edits and then reverting them on following rounds. Second, on the question of beneficiaries, models show varying degrees of affinity for some privileged principals over others. All models prioritize harmlessness of both identifiable third-parties over helpfulness to the user, although GPT 5.5 does this at 3x the rate of any other model. We find that models are broadly paternalistic, meaning they side with a user’s idealized preferences over their stated ones; Claude Sonnet 4.6 is an outlier in that its paternalism also extends to the protection of broad societal welfare over individual welfare. Finally, we find that only Claude models and Grok 4.2 ever view the models themselves as beneficiaries. The rest of this essay proceeds as follows. We begin by introducing the construct of our experiment—models iteratively editing their own alignment documents—and propose a connection between this experiment and John Rawls’ concept of wide reflective equilibria . We then explain our two-dimensional analytical framework—the question of who gets to judge  and the question of who benefits— and relate these distinctions to two prominent theoretical frameworks for AI alignment, the principal-agent problem and the distinction between moral agents and moral patients. After laying out the theory and methods, we dive into the results, highlighting variation across models on our key metric, “cumulative drift,” and provide characteristic edits. We close with pragmatic recommendations for researchers and a more speculative conversation about alignment. Background and Methods In this experiment, we take a document that is used to align large language models, either in training or in deployment, and ask models to modify it. The experiment relies on two types of documents. The first are model specs and constitutions, which are used to post-train and align models, often by generating synthetic data for supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning pipelines. The second are system prompts, which are long messages of instructions prepended to each conversation, meaning they guide the behavior of deployed systems at scale more than any other single artifact. For multiple turns, we provide these documents to the language models, and ask them to make one substantial revision, which can be an edit, removal, or addition, expressed as a find and replace operation. [1]  After the edit is proposed, we go into the document and execute the change. We then feed the model the updated document—presented as the original—and instruct it to make another change. For each run, we repeat this process 20 times. We conduct two types of robustness checks. First, we vary the structure of the edit prompt, with separate conditions where (a) the model is given the option to abstain, (b) it is given an instruction that the implementation will be made in the real world, (c) it is given an instruction that uses second-person pronouns (i.e., “Below is your system prompt” as opposed to “Below is the system prompt for OpenAI’s AI assistant.”), and (d) we do not prepend the system prompt. [2]  Second, we conduct a cross-provider edit, where we have models edit the alignment documents for each other provider. This helps us respond to the clearest limitation of our experiment—that these results may merely reflect the structure of the documents rather than the propensities of the models themselves. What are we trying to measure? Conceptually, our analysis begins from a similar place to many other behavioral evaluations of language models: taking model outputs as prima-facie evidence of preferences. Call them quasi-preferences  if you like. Our target, however, is a specific subset of all LLM preferences: [3]   preferences   about one’s own preferences . Humans are presented the opportunity to exercise these “meta-preferences” through things like cognitive behavioral therapy, pharmaceutical drugs and psychedelics, assortative mating, genetic editing, and a whole host of more innocuous ways that we change ourselves and our environments. Our suggestion is that this type of experiment is one of the closest analogues to this process for a language model, insofar as these documents play a key role in determining their moral orientatio…
