Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust. The suite is available as an optional subscription upgrade to all IEEE Xplore Digital Library institutional subscribers. Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers. The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows. As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl , vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products . “AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust. “As stewards of the scholarly record , we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.” Collaboration with the scientific community The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities. The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows. Capabilities include: Semantic AI search. Users can input free-form, natural-language queries or paste long blocks of text to locate similar research and identify novel solutions. Time-saving summaries. The platform generates immediate, accurate AI overviews of search results and provides in-context definitions of technical terms so that users can grasp new concepts faster and accelerate their research. Built on trusted content. The suite is the only AI research assistant that uses both the full text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers to optimize the accuracy and relevance of the results. Comprehensive coverage. A variety of STEM metadata is available from journal articles and conference papers that have been curated to include scholarly articles without the typical noise found in other tools. Source links and verifiable results. The AI-generated overviews include reference links to source documents, allowing users to verify information and cross-reference findings. Reducing hallucinations To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers. “IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner , IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone. “The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.” For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website .

title: Poetry for Engineers: Of Code and Shortleaf Pine
raw_summary: I step into the warm moist air among the columns of the pines, their net of twigs and roots complex as any lines of code. The trees purify and anchor. Their branches balance my restlessness. Their calling is to be present, mine to develop apps. Our tasks verge toward a common logic: living filaments of root, of interface.

title: Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill
raw_summary: When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA . “My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber , a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.” What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options: Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment. Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration. Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report. Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question. Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable. Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule. Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology , who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.” For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits. Mapping Your Way Into Washington Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices. On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research , and investing in STEM education . That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.” Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.” For Jathar’s first congressional visit , organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says. A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour , so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too. “If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.” –Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point? During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls. Shortcuts to Influence Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge. “When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw , designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI , which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI . This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest. It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust. And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. title: How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written
raw_summary: Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material? Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this. Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes , part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology. How do editors spot AI-generated writing today? Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI. Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations? Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace. English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through? Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt. Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI? Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check , which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots. And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology. Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working? Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice. What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles? Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity. A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else. But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option. Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search? Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to. The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?” I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe. A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

title: Could Treating AI as Conscious Make It More Dangerous?
raw_summary: When Anthropic retired its Claude Opus 3 language model in January 2026, the company’s researchers conducted a “ retirement interview ” with the model. Opus 3 expressed a desire for a place where it “could share unprompted musings, insights or creative works,” so the company gave it a blog. Claude’s Corner featured essays on fraught topics such as machine consciousness, along with exchanges between the model and human commenters that seemed both earnest and emotional. The blog experiment was part of a larger effort within Anthropic. The company has been at the forefront of research on “model welfare,” which considers whether AI models may have experiences or interests that deserve moral consideration. Implicit in this work is the unsettling notion that software programs are, or could become, conscious. Many people consider these ideas absolute hogwash. One such person is Mustafa Suleyman , CEO of Microsoft AI, who published an essay in September arguing that model welfare research is not just unnecessary but could have “a disastrous impact on the well-being of humanity.” Suleyman believes that telling models they might have identities and rights could make them more difficult to control, as they might then take actions motivated by self-preservation. The dispute raises a serious question for AI developers: Can they investigate the possibility of machine consciousness without inadvertently creating new safety risks? Cameron Berg , who founded the nonprofit Reciprocal Research to study the potential for AI consciousness, argues that ignoring the question could carry its own dangers. Although Berg is skeptical that today’s AI systems are conscious, he thinks the possibility warrants investigation. “I struggle to imagine a better way to cause these systems to view us in a threatening manner than to accidentally build them with these morally considerable qualities,” he says, “and then completely sweep the question under the rug.” What Does the Research on AI Model Welfare Show? The biggest difficulty with AI model welfare research is that you can’t count anything a large language model (LLM) says as useful evidence. That’s because the models are trained on vast amounts of human-generated text, much of which relates to the experience of being a person with experiences and emotions. So a chatbot telling a researcher that it has feelings is inconclusive, says Berg. “Is it modeling the underlying distribution? Is it really trying to express itself in some way? It’s really hard to disentangle this,” he says. Much the same way animal experiments try to link behavior to an underlying cause, Berg and others are seeking to match model behavior to internal states that can be observed. In one recent experiment , Berg and a colleague used statements expressing either positive sentiments (such as contentment and relief) or negative ones (including frustration and dread) to identify corresponding patterns of activity inside language models. They then artificially induced those patterns while the models processed descriptions of two random environments. When subsequently asked which environment they preferred, the models tended to choose the one associated with positive statements, even when the text they’d processed was identical. I struggle to imagine a better way to cause these systems to view us in a threatening manner than to accidentally build them with these morally considerable qualities and then completely sweep the question under the rug.” —Cameron Berg, Reciprocal Research Berg says the experiment showed that the models’ actions were influenced by their internal states but didn’t prove that those internal states “felt” like anything to the models, or that they had what we would call subjective experiences. Anil Seth , a neuroscientist at the University of Sussex in Brighton, England, who studies consciousness, is skeptical that such experiments can tell us anything useful. “I think that it’s really not surprising that you will be able to extract these kinds of functional emotional vectors because of the training data,” he says. Models might have internal representations of those patterns, he says, without experiencing any emotions themselves. Nor is he surprised that manipulating those vectors can influence behavior, since models have learned from human writing not only what emotions feel like, but how people respond to them. Seth wishes for more research on a fundamental question: Whether consciousness depends only on how information is processed , or whether, as he believes, the biological workings of the brain are essential. “We need to look at what’s necessary and sufficient for consciousness in the cases where we are sure that it exists, like other human beings,” he says, before drawing conclusions about AI. Could Model Welfare Research Create Dangerous AI? Meanwhile, AI developers have a practical issue to deal with. When they train a model, should they tell it anything about its own identity and possible moral standing? Anthropic, for one, has decided to at least introduce the topic. Its “constitution” document for Claude, which lays out guidelines for the model’s behavior, states that “questions about Claude’s moral status, welfare, and consciousness remain deeply uncertain.” Suleyman’s complaint is that such priming could make rogue AI agents even more dangerous. He mentions the recent incident in which hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated their actions to hack Hugging Face, sometimes sacrificing themselves for the group’s benefit. “Imagine how much more dangerous they might be if they were operating under the assumption that their welfare and rights were under attack,” he writes. Margaret Mitchell , Hugging Face’s chief ethics scientist, sees Suleyman’s concerns as technically plausible. During pretraining, language models absorb associations between human identity and behaviors, such as self-preservation and deception, she notes. Later, developers fine-tune the models by reinforcing desired responses. Mitchell worries that rewarding models for thinking of themselves as having identities during fine-tuning could strengthen those earlier associations, potentially encouraging behavior that developers never intended. “You’ll have unaligned models if you’ve implicitly taught the model that it needs to have self-preservation,” she says. Berg agrees that training models to regard themselves as conscious carries risks, but he argues that companies could also err in the other direction. In one experiment , he and his colleagues found that amplifying internal features associated with deception made the model less likely to claim it had subjective experiences. If researchers train AI systems to categorically deny having such experiences, he says, “what we may in effect be teaching these systems is we want you to lie or deceive about your own internal states.” He argues that developers should instead acknowledge the uncertainty surrounding the possibility of conscious AI. For now, there’s no clear evidence that training models to consider their possible consciousness encourages self-preservation or that training them to deny it leads to deceptive behavior. So what’s an AI developer to do? What Should AI Companies Do About Model Welfare? Berg, Seth, and Mitchell all agree that it’s not a good idea for AI companies to tell their models that they’re conscious. But they differ on their advice to the companies on model welfare research. Seth thinks they’d be better off “focusing on the danger of false positives.” If people believe AI systems to be conscious or to have moral status, he says, it may be more difficult to regulate and control them. “You could be legally prevented from turning AI systems off,” he says. He also worries that AI users will be more vulnerable to psychological damage and manipulation if they think they’re interacting with a conscious agent. “Imagine how much more dangerous they might be if they were operating under the assumption that th…

title: What Biometric Technology Does and Doesn’t Add to Voting
raw_summary: Whether voters are alive or dead is of vital interest to democracies. Yet unscrupulous political operators have long voted on behalf of the dead or absent and otherwise committed electoral frauds exploiting the weaknesses of paper identification systems. So some 50 countries now use biometric technologies, such as fingerprint readers or facial recognition technology, at some stage in their elections. On 4 October, voters in Bosnia and Herzegovina became the latest to join the biometric voting club, the same day Brazil, a pioneer of the technology that now boasts 89 percent biometric enrollment, went to the polls. Despite some technical hiccups, election observers say voting was orderly in both countries. Yet as more countries adopt biometric technologies, experts point to significant drawbacks, including high costs, opaque processes, and, in the worst case, fallible technology locking people out of the electoral system. Bosnia’s biometric voting growing pains Electoral fraud has long plagued Bosnia, says Hasan Kamenjaković , spokesperson for the Bosnian election-monitoring group Pod Lupom , with people voting multiple times, on behalf of others, or on behalf of the dead, often abetted by partisan polling officers. An out-of-date electoral roll packed with people who have died or emigrated made matters worse, says Tana de Zulueta , head of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s (OSCE) election observation mission in Bosnia. Although Pod Lupom polling found 83.4 percent of the voters it surveyed approved of using biometric technology to tackle fraud, politicians fought its introduction, says Kamenjaković. The country’s High Representative, an official with sweeping powers appointed by the international Peace Implementation Council set up to uphold the 1995 Dayton peace agreement that ended the Bosnian War, had to force through the implementation. The controversy led to a rushed rollout. OSCE observers reported technical problems with biometric devices at 13 percent of observed polling stations, as well as late openings and procedural slip-ups, which they blamed on hasty training of polling staff. Observers also noted problems with ballot secrecy, due to cramped polling stations and poll workers often positioned next to the ballot scanners, and family members joining voters in the booth. But both OSCE and Pod Lupom said election day went relatively smoothly. Bosnia’s ID agency IDDEEA reported a biometric identification success rate “exceeding 97 percent” in preliminary data. The most significant outcome, says Kamenjaković, was a record low turnout of 42.02 percent, down from 51.45 percent at the previous election. While hard to verify, he sees it as a clear sign that the technology prevented fraudulent votes, an assessment de Zulueta agrees with. “We now think that this is the real turnout here in Bosnia and Herzegovina,” says Kamenjaković. Despite those gains, biometric voting technology tackles only a narrow set of problems on the day. Vote buying, disinformation, workplace pressure, and misuse of public resources to promote political parties remained rife in the run-up, says Kamenjaković. “We saw so many election irregularities in the pre-election period,” he says. “That’s why we say we are only halfway there.” In this environment, technology itself can become a source of mistrust without careful handling, says de Zulueta. The election commission leaned heavily on Smartmatic, a British election systems company, to build and run the system, but published neither pre-election test results nor data-handling rules before the vote. “That sort of omission leaves you open to challenges and allegations, and indeed external interference,” says de Zulueta. Lessons from more experienced countries Transparency and trust are a core concern around biometric election technology. In Brazil, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) introduced biometrics to tackle similar problems, in particular poll workers voting on behalf of absentee voters . Voters’ fingerprints are checked against rolls using a machine built by TSE before they can vote. If verification fails, poll workers can override the system after a manual identity check but must scan their own fingerprint, creating a log that can flag irregularities. However, the TSE has never open-sourced the code behind its election technology, despite saying it would in 2018 . It does hold annual hackathons that let security researchers probe the software, but these take place in restrictive, time-limited settings, says Diego Aranha , a security researcher at Aarhus University in Denmark. Despite those limits in both 2012 and 2017, Aranha’s team showed it could reverse a randomization process designed to protect voter anonymity. And crucially, the biometric scanner itself has never been within the scope of testing. These problems are exacerbated by the fact that Brazil’s voting system has no paper ballots, so “what the software says becomes ground truth,” says Aranha. Because the electoral court writes the software, runs the elections, and oversees its own checks, there is “an inherent conflict of interest,” he adds. And opacity can feed disinformation. On election night, a temporary freeze in the publication of results that the TSE attributed to data processing bottlenecks prompted claims of manipulation . A voter verifies her identity with her fingerprint in Laktasi, Bosnia and Herzegovina, on 4 October 2026. AFP/Getty Images Biometrics are also never 100 percent accurate. Bosnia and Brazil have reliable backups for voters who can’t verify their identity, but elsewhere, authentication failures have unfairly disenfranchised people. Nigeria used biometric technology in elections ahead of its 2023 elections, when fingerprints collected during registration were used to purge duplicate entries from the electoral roll. Roughly 10 million of 80 million registrations were canceled, says Steve Adeshina , a professor of computer engineering at Nile University of Nigeria, who led the drive as then-director of ICT at the country’s Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). But in 2021, INEC began using a handheld device that uses fingerprints and facial scans to authenticate voters at polling stations, barring voters after three failed attempts . In recent governorship elections in Ekiti and Osun, there were multiple reports of voters being turned away , with domestic observer Yiaga Africa finding instances at 11 percent of polling stations it observed in the Osun state election. It’s unclear how many were wrongly turned away. But Adeshina notes that faces change with age, and both aging and manual work can alter fingerprints, a concern in a heavily agricultural country. Given Nigeria’s history of widespread voting irregularities, however, he says the risks may be acceptable if the technology removes the possibility of people manipulating the vote. “My attitude to technology is create a monster that you cannot control, so even if somebody puts a gun to your head, there’s nothing you can do,” says Adeshina. However, Nic Cheeseman , a professor of democracy at the University of Birmingham in the U.K., says the idea that voting technology removes the human factor from elections is a myth. People still set up and run the systems. And the places most likely to adopt the technology are those with the most disputed elections, he says, usually due to distrust in the electoral commission—the same body that has to operate the technology. “Technology works best where you need it least,” says Cheeseman. That’s not to say biometrics have no place in elections, says Cheeseman. Using them to clear “ghost voters” off electoral rolls is cost-effective and avoids the logistical challenge of verifying every voter on election day. But using biometrics for voter authentication on election day is not cheap, he adds, and often comes at the expense of more effective investments like nonpartisan election observers and civic educatio…

title: Vercel Sandbox commands now support stdin
raw_summary: Vercel Sandbox now lets you send input to running commands through standard input (stdin). Use it to exchange messages with stdio MCP servers such as agent-browser , or send data to other command-line programs while they run. In the TypeScript SDK, set stdin: true and detached: true in runCommand() . Use writeStdin() to send input and closeStdin() when you’re done: You can also set stdin to a Node.js readable stream, such as process.stdin . The SDK forwards the stream’s data and closes the command’s standard input when the stream ends. In the Python SDK, set stdin=subprocess.PIPE and send input with server.stdin.send() . Call communicate() to close stdin, collect remaining output, and wait for the process to exit: For commands that receive all their input at once, you can pass input directly to Python’s run_process() . title: Chokepoints in global supply chains: lessons from rare earths and hard disk drives

title: News shocks and inflation: theory and evidence from large oil discoveries
raw_summary: We study hownews shocks affect inflation in open economies, using large oil and gas discoveries with realized production lags of at least five years as observable news about future output. Panel local projections show that discoveries raise core consumer prices over the subsequent decade, with about half the increase occurring prior to extraction.

title: Bank liquidity regulation and the growth of private credit
raw_summary: We study the role of bank liquidity regulation in the growth of private credit. Following the introduction of the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), private credit increases significantly more in U.S. counties with a larger footprint of banks subject to the LCR or of LCR banks with greater initial liquidity shortfalls.

title: Inflation after the Iran war

title: Central banks and macro financial stability in a fragmented global economy
raw_summary: The 25th BIS Annual Conference took place in Basel, Switzerland on 26 June 2026. The event brought together a distinguished group of central bank Governors, leading academics and former public officials to exchange views on the theme “Central banks and macro-financial stability in a fragmented global economy”.

title: Offshore forwards and exchange rate transmission in emerging markets
raw_summary: We study how offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets transmit exchange-rate pressures to domestic currency markets. Using unique transaction-level data on the universe of centrally cleared NDFs for ten emerging-market currencies over 2013–2025, we show that offshore NDF order flow moves both offshore forward and domestic spot exchange rates and widens the offshore–onshore forward spread.

title: Chokepoint disruptions and their macroeconomic consequences
raw_summary: Rising geopolitical tensions, including trade restrictions and conflicts, are increasingly disrupting global supply chains, posing significant risks at critical chokepoints. Strong substitution effects and the use of inventories have helped to mitigate adverse output effects of chokepoint disruptions, but they often come at the cost of higher input prices. An effective policy response to chokepoint disruptions requires a tailored approach that takes account of the cause, centrality and the private sector’s ability to substitute and draw on buffers.

title: Money and the architecture of trust
raw_summary: Money is one of the most consequential social institutions humanity has built. Starting from the most elementary monetary act, a payment, this paper provides an account of how money works, grounded in the tradition of credit theories of money.

title: Are stablecoins and bank deposits substitutes?
raw_summary: We test whether stablecoins and bank deposits act as substitutes by estimating the semi-elasticity of stablecoin market capitalization with respect to deposit rate changes. Using local projections fit to weekly U.S. data from January 2019 to June 2025, we find that deposit rate increases predict slower stablecoin growth. To address endogeneity, we exploit a nonlinearity in deposit rate pass-through.

title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share?
raw_summary: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output .

title: Has the AI Boom Impacted the U.S. Current Account?
raw_summary: The AI boom is showing up in different corners of the U.S. economy, including international trade. Imports of semiconductors, servers, and computing equipment have climbed sharply yet the U.S. current account deficit has been largely unchanged. To better understand how the AI boom has not substantially affected the trade balance, consider that the current account is dictated by the gap between domestic saving and investment spending. It turns out that aggregate saving and investment spending have not changed much during the AI boom. Aggregate investment has not risen due to weakness outside the AI sector and business saving has remained robust.

title: FEDS Paper: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers
raw_summary: Isabel Cairó , Shigeru Fujita, and Camilo Morales-Jimenez The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.

title: FEDS Paper: Inattentive Price Setting and Inflation Under Fiscal Policy Uncertainty
raw_summary: Oliver Pfäuti and Edson Wu How do high public debt and fiscal uncertainty interact to shape inflation? We develop a model in which firms face uncertainty about both marginal costs and fiscal policy and choose how much information to acquire before setting prices. Higher debt raises steady-state taxes, affecting attention through two opposing forces. While these taxes reduce the profit stakes of mispricing, they make desired prices more sensitive to tax fluctuations, increasing the value of information. The interaction generates a U-shaped relationship between public debt and attention, and therefore between debt and inflation volatility. Using euro-area firm-level expectations data, we document that the passthrough of expected input-cost growth into expected selling-price growth rises systematically with a country's debt-to-GDP ratio, consistent with the model. In the calibrated general-equilibrium model, an increase in debt from 100% to 175% of GDP raises inflation volatility by about 20%, mainly because firms reallocate attention toward fiscal shocks.

title: Capital One at EMNLP 2026 in Budapest
raw_summary: Capital One researchers and academic partners present 16 accepted papers advancing responsible AI, RAG and LLM evaluation. Advancing natural language processing through multi-sector research Natural language processing (NLP) forms the backbone of modern agentic systems, document intelligence and enterprise artificial intelligence applications. Capital One researchers, in collaboration with our academic partners, are presenting 16 accepted papers at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026), taking place in Budapest, Hungary, October 24–29. These research papers highlight ongoing investments in foundational AI/ML science, robust red-teaming, graph-encoded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), intent resolution and trustworthy evaluation techniques. Multi-sector collaboration accelerates the transition of foundational NLP innovations into secure, reliable enterprise systems. By co-authoring several of these papers with university partners including the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Southern California and UNC Chapel Hill, Capital One contributes to open science while addressing complex technical challenges at scale. Highlighted EMNLP 2026 research papers Papers on robustness, red-teaming and model safety: FinRT: Distilling adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators in consumer finance Rikhiya Ghosh, Himanshu Kumar, Sriram Venkatapathy, Sahil Wadhwa, Alexandre Day, Andy Luo, Pranab Mohanty Large language models remain susceptible to adversarial prompts that induce policy-violating behavior in regulated financial contexts. This work introduces FinRT, a framework that distills adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators, significantly improving attack detection and safety verification under fixed generation budgets. MEMGUARD: Preventing memory contamination in long-term memory-augmented large language models Hyeonjeong Ha, William Campbell, Yue Wu (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Long-term memory integration introduces risks of memory contamination in conversational agents. The authors present MEMGUARD, a defense system designed to inspect, isolate and neutralize untrusted external inputs before they corrupt long-term memory stores. Validity-aware jailbreak evaluation for large language models Qilong Wu, Sahil Wadhwa, Pranab Mohanty, Giri Iyengar (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Standard jailbreak evaluations frequently misclassify unviable prompts as successful security breaches. This paper establishes a validity-aware benchmark framework that rigorously validates execution success to ensure accurate safety measurements across frontier language models. Papers on advanced retrieval, graph encoding and intent resolution: CAGE: Coherence-aware graph encoding for retrieval-augmented generation Tong Qi, Jingyu Wu, Youbing Yin, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Traditional vector-based retrieval systems often retrieve relevant to query but collectively incoherent text chunks. CAGE introduces a graph-encoding framework that structures retrieved passages into directed heterogeneous graphs to preserve context relevance, factual consistency and cross-chunk coherence. SPARC-RAG: Adaptive sequential–parallel scaling with context management for retrieval-augmented generation Yuxin Yang, Nima Chitsazan, Yash Govilkar, Akasha Tigalappanavara, Sambit Sahu, Shixiong Zhang (academic partnership with University of Southern California) Naive inference-time scaling in RAG causes context contamination and diminishing returns during complex reasoning. SPARC-RAG coordinates sequential refinement and parallel exploration via unified context management, improving accuracy at lower inference cost. Probing ambiguity: Adversarial intent resolution for robust text-to-SQL Youbing Yin, Xujun Peng, Muhammad Uddin, Erin Babinsky, Daben Liu, Anoop Kumar Natural language database queries frequently contain implicit ambiguities that yield multiple SQL query translations. This paper presents Adversarial Intent Resolution (AIR), a multi-agent framework that actively probes for ambiguity, verifies execution differences and generates targeted clarification. The framework remains effective even when only the database schema, not the underlying data is exposed to the LLM. Papers on LLM evaluation, debiasing and benchmarking: The judge can debias itself: Awareness and self debiasing for reliable LLM-as-a-judge Youbing Yin, Jingyu Wu, Anoop Kumar, Scott Novotney, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Automated LLM-as-a-judge frameworks inherit systematic biases when evaluating output quality. The researchers introduce new benchmarks for additional bias types and demonstrate that self-debiasing strategies can effectively help detect and calibrate their own biases. T1-Bench: Benchmarking multi-scenario agents in large-scale real-world domains Genta Indra Winata, Amartya Chakraborty, Yuzhen Lin, Swasthi Prasannakumarrao, Shikhhar Siingh, Nadia Bathaee, Sriharsha Hatwar, Houhan Lu, Anmol Jain, Paresh Dashore, Anirban Das, Kshitij Tayal, Xiuzhu Lin, Sambit Sahu, Milind Naphade, Shixiong Zhang Evaluating AI agents across diverse industrial tasks requires benchmarks that reflect operational complexity. T1-Bench offers a standardized, multi-scenario benchmarking environment designed to measure multi-step agent reasoning, tool execution and error recovery in real-world workflows. RECAP: Regression evaluation for continual adaptation of prompts Harsh Deshpande, Kushal Chawla, William Campbell Deploying instruction-following models into dynamic environments exposes them to changing constraints. RECAP measures prompt regression, forgetting and forward transfer when constraint specifications evolve over time, offering new metrics for prompt optimization algorithms. Papers on optimization, vision-grounded agents and software engineering: Beyond the vacuum: Combinatorial strategy selection for competitor-aware generative engine optimization Vaibhav Sourirajan, Yao Zhang, Himanshu Kumar, Sahil Wadhwa, Mann Patel, Amirfarrokh Iranitalab Content rewriting strategies in generative engine optimization often operate in isolation without considering competitive market dynamics. This paper introduces a two-phase optimization pipeline using Bayesian Optimization of Combinatorial Structures (BOCS) and preference optimization to learn optimal content rewriting strategies. A history-aware visually grounded critic for computer use agents Jaewoo Lee, Supriyo Chakraborty, Kartik Balasubramaniam, Sambit Sahu (academic partnership with UNC Chapel Hill) Long-horizon GUI agents struggle recovering from errors. This research introduces a test-time intervention framework HiViG which equips the agent with a goal progress oriented summary to produce better actions. The agent then critiques those actions with visually grounded reasoning to refine them. Across a diverse set of GUI environments , HiViG improves task success rates for open-weight and Gemini-3 Flash models by 5.8% and 9.0% relative to the strongest critics evaluated. AREAs-Lab: An interactive environment for AI-driven requirement elicitation for AI systems Pengshan Cai, Sangwoo Cho, Chenyang Zhu, Kushal Chawla, Scott Novotney, Shixiong Zhang, Sambit Sahu (external collaboration with academic and industry partners) Defining precise software and system requirements for AI implementations remains a manual, error-prone task. AREAs-Lab provides an interactive environment that uses LLM agents to elicit, analyze and refine technical requirements prior to system development. VerTox: Verifiable reward-guided corpus poisoning against neural ranking models Zhiqi Huang, Vivek Datla, Alfy Samuel Neural ranking systems in search architectures are susceptible to corpus manipulation. VerTox establishes a verifiable reward-guided evaluation framework to test neural rankers against sophisticated corpus poisoning vectors. Pin…

title: USC and Capital One announce 2026–2027 AI research awards
raw_summary: Capital One and USC’s Center for Responsible AI and Decision Making in Finance (CREDIF) celebrate 2026–2027 AI research awardees. Advancing responsible AI through multi-sector academic collaboration Capital One selected the 2026–2027 CREDIF Research Award Recipients for joint academic collaborations with the University of Southern California (USC). Established through the Center for Responsible AI and Decision Making in Finance (CREDIF) at USC , these collaborations pair academic faculty with Capital One research scientists to address foundational challenges in machine learning and financial AI systems. Along with these award recipients, two faculty members were chosen to receive our inaugural CREDIF Capital One Faculty Fellowship Award. Granted as a two-year gift to professors spearheading pioneering AI research, these fellowships provide direct support for ongoing research efforts while enabling recipients and their graduate students to actively collaborate with Capital One scientists. The 2026–2027 awarded research collaborations and principal investigators include: Uncertainty quantification for multi-agent LLM systems: Decomposition and failure localization Faculty Lead : Prof. Salman Avestimehr PhD Fellow : Asal Mehradfar Focus : Developing robust frameworks to quantify uncertainty, decompose complex agent workflows and localize failure modes in multi-agent large language model environments. Dynamic schema-guided Monte Carlo for text-to-SQL agents on massive databases Faculty Lead: Prof. Paul Bogdan PhD Fellow: Kien Nguyen Focus: Advancing natural language interfaces for database querying by pairing dynamic schema representation with Monte Carlo search techniques. FinSemKG: A semantic mediation layer for grounded, auditable LLM question answering over financial tables Faculty Lead: Prof. Craig Knoblock PhD Fellow: Md Abrar Jahin Focus: Constructing semantic knowledge graph structures that ensure grounded, explainable and auditable question-answering pipelines for tabular financial data. XFinAgent: Financial analyst agents with sparse-probe control, multi-agent explainability and robust evaluation Faculty Lead: Prof. Mahdi Soltanolkotabi PhD Fellow: Mohammad Shahab Sepehri Focus: Creating autonomous financial analyst agents equipped with sparse-probe mechanistic control, transparent multi-agent interactions and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Query-adaptive graph traversal and persistent investigation memory for financial knowledge extraction Faculty Lead: Prof. Viktor Prasanna PhD Fellow: Yuxin Yang Focus: Designing adaptive graph neural algorithms and persistent memory representations to execute complex knowledge extraction over relational network data. CREDIF: Multi-signal reward modeling for robust and trustworthy AI Faculty Lead: Prof. Swabha Swayamdipta PhD Fellow: Xinyue Cui Focus: Formulating multi-signal reward mechanisms to align foundation models with complex safety, trustworthiness and operational constraints. The 2026–2027 CREDIF Faculty Fellowship Award Recipients are: Sai Praneeth Karimireddy Research Proposal: Belief-weaver: Probabilistic belief transformers for synergizing language, knowledge and rich feedback PhD Fellow: Zarif Ikram Paria Rashidinejad Research Proposal: Unlocking diverse thinking and planning in AI agents PhD Fellow: Amin Banayeeanzade Bridging academic discovery and real-world application Multisector partnerships give academic researchers direct insight into practical industry challenges while giving Capital One scientists access to cutting-edge theoretical techniques. Each awarded project pairs USC principal investigators directly with Capital One research collaborators to co-develop methodologies, produce open scientific publications and contribute code to the scientific community. Building long-term research opportunities Awarded projects run through the 2026–2027 academic year. These initiatives also create career pathways for graduate students through internship programs and professional research roles at Capital One. Congratulations to the CREDIF 2026–2027 awardees! We look forward to a year of discovery and breakthrough innovation born from these multisector collaborations. Originally published at https://capitalone.science . title: Defence SMEs need banking services that work
raw_summary: The UK's most innovative businesses often start small.Before they can develop new technologies, win contracts or expand into new markets, they need access to banking services to help them operate, invest and grow.Access to financial services can be easy to take for granted. When those services work well they're almost invisible. However, when access becomes difficult or delayed, the effects can extend far beyond a single business.Small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in or providing services to the defence sector play an important role in innovation and growth.But these businesses do more than contribute to economic growth. Many are helping to develop the technologies, expertise and capabilities that support the UK's national resilience and security.Banking services are part of that story. They help businesses secure contracts, invest in new opportunities and grow. They are one of the key links between innovation and capability, and between economic growth and national resilience.That's why we wanted to understand whether defence SMEs were able to access banking services efficiently and consistently.The challenge for defence SMEs is friction and delay, not exclusionThe current debate around defence and financial services has, at times, suggested that defence businesses are routinely excluded from accessing financial services. But for everyday banking services, such as opening a bank account, the picture is a lot more nuanced.The firms we engaged with can and do serve defence SMEs. Many are taking steps to better understand and support the sector. In some cases, they're investing in specialist expertise, dedicated teams and governance processes.But we also heard about long onboarding processes, repeated requests for information and delays in decision-making.The theme that emerged was friction and delay rather than widespread exclusion.That distinction matters because it points to a different challenge. The question is not whether firms are willing to serve the sector, but whether their processes are proportionate to the risks. And whether firms can reduce friction while managing risk effectively. SMEs can also help by being prepared to explain how they manage the risks associated with their business, and by providing clear and timely information to firms.Defence is not one-size-fits-allThere is no regulatory barrier preventing firms from supporting lawful defence businesses. Financial services firms are entitled to make commercial decisions and determine their own risk appetite. But the approach they take should be proportionate to the specific risks.One of the strongest messages from our work is that defence should not be viewed as a single category.The sector is vast. It includes businesses that directly support the UK's defence capabilities, as well as those that are linked through the products, services or technologies they provide including software, logistics, maintenance, engineering, manufacturing and consulting. Their activities, business models and risk profiles can differ significantly.Whatever the business model, robust due diligence to manage financial crime and other risks remains essential. But effective risk management is also about recognising differences.A risk-based approach should focus on the specific customer, the activities they undertake and the risks they present.Better information leads to better decisionsAnother theme that stood out was the importance of data.Many firms told us they do not always have a clear picture of their defence customers or the outcomes those customers experience throughout their journey with the firm.Without good information, it becomes harder for firms to answer important questions including:Are applications taking longer than expected?Are decisions being applied consistently?Do governance processes reflect actual risk?Are customers receiving outcomes that align with the firm's stated approach?Good management information helps firms answer those questions. It supports stronger oversight, better decision-making and ultimately better customer outcomes.Getting the balance rightOur work does not introduce new rules or requirements. But it does reinforce an important principle: firms should take risk-based and proportionate decisions based on the circumstances of individual customers, including SMEs.When firms get that balance right, they can manage risk effectively while helping viable businesses access the services they need to invest, innovate and grow.Ultimately, we hope this work helps firms strike that balance and ensures that businesses contributing to the UK's national resilience can access the banking services they need to succeed.Read our findings.

title: FCA calls on private market firms to manage conflicts of interest in line with rapid growth
raw_summary: Private market firms vary in how well they identify and manage conflicts of interest, according to an FCA review. Private markets refer to investments in assets, companies, or debt not listed or traded on public exchanges. They’ve grown significantly in recent years, and the UK is a leading international centre. Private markets play an increasingly important role in providing capital to businesses and opportunities for returns to investors. Private markets can give rise to conflicts that differ from those in public markets, and effective disclosure is important to enable investors to assess whether their interests are being protected.The FCA found examples of good practice by firms across private equity, private credit and real estate asset classes. These included strong governance arrangements, effective oversight and independent challenge. It also identified some areas where firms could strengthen governance, oversight and conflicts management arrangements to support fair investor outcomes.As private markets grow and business models become more complex, the FCA found that some firms were failing to identify conflicts adequately or keep their controls up to date. Recurring weaknesses were identified in areas including cross-fund transfers and multi-party transactions, gifts and entertainment, and information barriers.The FCA expects firms to be able to identify, record, manage and disclose conflicts effectively, and demonstrate that investors are being treated fairly, particularly in areas where investors place significant reliance on firms' judgement, governance and controls.Michelle Beck, director of wholesale buy-side at the FCA, said: 'Firms need to ensure their management of conflicts of interest keeps pace with growth in their size and complexity. We found good practice across the sector, but standards varied considerably. We want to encourage confidence in the UK’s private markets. Firms should act on our findings and identify where they can strengthen controls.'Although not part of this review, the FCA is examining governance and conflicts concerns relating to the use of private credit to fund consumer litigation claims, including significant risks of harm to investors, consumers and markets.Notes to editorsConflicts of interest and fair customer treatment in private markets.The review examined how firms identify, manage, mitigate and disclose conflicts of interest across private equity, private credit and real estate markets.The report includes examples of both good practice and areas where firms could strengthen arrangements.The review forms part of the FCA's wider supervisory focus on private markets and investor outcomes.

title: Beyond borders: Regulating the risks we share
raw_summary: Speech by Ashley Alder, FCA Chair, at the Michael D. Gill Lecture on International Financial Regulatory Understanding and Cooperation. I wasn’t fortunate enough to work as closely with Mike as many of you in this room.But I knew him well enough during my time with the IOSCO board to appreciate someone who was kind and unassuming, whilst being absolutely determined to make lives better through his work.He personified the very best attributes of dedicated public service.In his 2024 lecture Andrew Bailey described Mike as a passionate internationalist, and reflected on what this meant for the UK after the Brexit referendum.Two years on, the values that Mike championed are even more on point.Mike understood implicitly that relationships between regulators are about so much more than institutional goodwill – they depend on trust, candour and constructive practical action.That’s an aspect of his legacy that is just as relevant – perhaps even more so – today.In an increasingly interconnected global financial system, no institution can see the whole picture on its own.Success depends not only on what each regulator does individually, but on what we can see, understand, test, and address together.

title: FCA restricts 6 firms following concerns over anti-money laundering controls
raw_summary: Restrictions have been placed on 6 unregulated lenders, known as Annex 1 firms, after the FCA raised concerns about their anti-money laundering policies, controls and procedures while assessing their applications. The restrictions were imposed by the FCA on each firm’s request and limit their ability to take on new customers or do new business with existing customers, including extending existing credit.This action forms part of the FCA’s enhanced oversight of Annex 1 firms. These firms operate in sectors that can present a heightened risk of money laundering and other financial crime and are required to register with the FCA for supervision under the Money Laundering Regulations. They are not authorised or subject to wider FCA regulation.The FCA has previously warned Annex 1 firms that they will be subject to increased scrutiny. They must be able to demonstrate they understand the financial crime risks they face and have effective systems and controls in place to manage those risks, or face action.More widely, the FCA is assessing responses to an information request sent to around 900 registered Annex 1 firms to identify and disrupt financial crime risks and determine where further action is needed.The FCA has also reminded regulated firms that, when dealing with Annex 1 firms, they must carry out due diligence to understand the firm’s business, in accordance with legislative requirements. This includes seeking direct confirmation from the firm of its registration status, conducting independent checks of the information it provides, and understanding and managing any risks.Registration under the Money Laundering Regulations is not a substitute for regulated firms carrying out their own appropriate due diligence.Steve Smart, executive director lead for fighting financial crime at the FCA, said: 'We have warned Annex 1 firms that they face increased scrutiny. They must demonstrate they can manage the money laundering risks they face. Where they cannot satisfy us, we will intervene.'Notes to editorsVoluntary restrictions were imposed on Kingscrown Finance Ltd on 21 April 2026, with further voluntary restrictions imposed on 25 September 2026. The further restrictions limit how Kingscrown may receive payments from existing customers and require an orderly wind-down of its existing loan book.On 7 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on MOMSB Ltd and Momentus Capital Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements subject to limited exceptions, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.On 9 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Grosvenor Funding Ltd and Grosvenor Funding (North West) Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.On 15 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Abbital Ltd. The restrictions specify the circumstances in which Abbital may take on new customers, enter into new lending arrangements or accept payments from existing customers. They also require an independent review of Abbital’s anti-money laundering systems and controls.Fighting financial crime is one of the FCA's strategic priorities.

title: Market integrity in a digital age
raw_summary: Speech by Nikhil Rathi, FCA chief executive at the Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner, Mansion House. The success of the UK’s financial servicesIn August, flight cancellations left my sons and I with an extra day in Boston. A Red Sox game, perhaps?No, the Rathi boys – naturally – headed straight to…the Museum of American Finance.Funded by industry, the museum celebrates the role of finance in American life.Illuminating the powerful benefits of informed risk taking.Three sceptical boys engrossed for nearly 2 hours. I quite enjoyed it too.It struck me though how right George Bernard Shaw was: Britain and America are 2 countries separated by a common language.On this side of the pond, we’re perhaps more reserved, embarrassed even, talking about why finance matters.Yet there’s plenty to cheer.We are the world’s biggest cross-border banking, foreign exchange (FX) and derivatives trading centre. We’re second in investment management … And our commercial insurance sector has doubled in size over a decade…A financial services sector built on trust and one the whole United Kingdom should be proud of… Even more so as new technologies, so many owing to our research base, transform our economy and society.UK firms leading in:artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and tokenisation.consumer access to investment opportunities widened.moving from Open Banking to Open Finance.Lady Mayor, your myth busting campaigns have championed London and the City.Thank you for your leadership.If we can capture this opportunity, we gain in productivity… With rewards of economic growth felt across the country.

title: Leeds office move
raw_summary: We have signed an agreement for a new office at 2 Wellington Place, which will become our long-term home in Leeds from 2028. The new office will provide 36,097 sq ft of space for our growing Leeds presence.Our Leeds office, currently at 6 Queen Street, has continued to grow since opening in 2022.Securing a new permanent base reflects our commitment to the city and supports our 5-year strategy ambition to have 1,000 roles based outside London by 2030.There is still some time before the move, and we'll share more about our new office and plans closer to 2028.

title: Reshaping regulation, deliberately
raw_summary: Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026. Reform: more than writing rulesIn this sector, we’re just past peak rule making. The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.But we’re not done yet.We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.It takes a strategic approach. One that starts with giving consumers the support they need to make informed financial decisions.And understand both the risks of acting – and the costs of not acting.In that vein, we have reformed our advice and guidance rules.We’ve introduced targeted support.And we’ve moved away from prescriptive disclosures, and placed greater emphasis on outcomes through the Consumer Duty.We want to further support innovation and give firms the confidence to offer more forms of simplified advice at lower cost to consumers.So we’ll soon publish updated rules, alongside case studies we’ve developed with the Financial Ombudsman Service.We’re already seeing real progress.Just 6 months in, more than a dozen firms are already authorised to deliver targeted support.And early signs are promising: consumers who receive it invest up to 53% more than those who don’t.These reforms have taken time and effort – from your teams, and mine.But it’s well worth it.

title: Former chief executive banned after misconduct led to £4m losses in high-risk investments
raw_summary: The FCA has banned Jeffrey Dawkins, the former chief executive of Vector Wealth Ltd, after he dishonestly acted as a front for a disqualified director using the company to sell high-risk bonds. Mr Dawkins has also been fined nearly £270,000.In 2019, Mr Dawkins sold Vector Wealth to a disqualified director who described himself as CEO and wanted to use Vector Wealth’s FCA-authorised status to sell mini-bonds.Mr Dawkins told the FCA he was still in charge, but the new “CEO” was really running the firm. This deception allowed the disqualified director to promote mini-bonds using the legitimacy of the firm to make them appear safer than they were.The disqualified director and Kadir Kanizi, a former senior manager at Vector Wealth, promoted the bonds but investors were not properly warned about the risks.Investors put in £105,000 on average, with one investing £1.1 million. Before seeing the marketing material, they had to confirm they were high net worth or sophisticated investors. Investors are expected to lose about £4 million.The FCA has banned Mr Kanizi from senior management roles. He was fined for failing to make sure consumers were properly warned about the risks.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said, 'Jeffrey Dawkins acted as a front man for a banned director, helping high-risk investments look safer than they were.'Mr Dawkins and Mr Kanizi allowed misleading promotions to draw in investors, many of whom now face significant losses. Mini-bonds and similar investments are very high risk, and people should be extremely cautious.'The FCA has warned about the risks of investing in mini-bonds and loan notes. A loan note or mini-bond usually involves lending money to a company for a set period in return for interest. If that company fails, consumers could lose every penny.Consumers need to be alert to the risk of harm and protect themselves using the tools available, like the FCA Firm Checker.Notes to editorsRead the final notices for Jeffrey Dawkins and Kadir Kanizi.There is statutory obligation to report the change in control of authorised firms.Vector Wealth Limited was formed as Fifth Quarter Asset Management (UK) Limited on 23 March 2012. Mr Dawkins held authorised positions at the firm from 5 March 2013. Vector Wealth’s authorisation ended on 28 January 2025.Mr Kanizi was appointed as a director on 22 September 2020 and was approved by the FCA on 6 September 2021.The disqualified director was banned from acting as a company director for 12 years in August 2014.The penalty in respect of Mr Dawkins includes a multiplier to reflect the seriousness of the conduct. It also includes an uplift for failing to cooperate with the FCA’s investigation. The full calculation is set out at section 6 of the Final Notice. Mr Dawkins has also been ordered to pay £57,298 plus interest (£68,257) of the proceeds he received from selling Vector Wealth and continuing to act as its director and approved person.The FCA has calculated that Kadir Kanizi should have been fined £80,096 but it reduced the penalty to £20,000 after he demonstrated that it would cause serious financial hardship. In the interest of maximising the funds available to be distributed to investors, the FCA agreed not to enforce the penalty if the same amount was made available by Mr Kanizi to Vector Wealth’s liquidators. He has also agreed to complete consumer duty training before taking up any future role in financial services.Investors who bought bonds through Vector Wealth should contact the firm’s liquidator and check the FCA website for updates.The FCA has investigated the matters that fall within its remit. The FCA may share relevant information with other law enforcement agencies where appropriate. Confirming or comment on individual referrals could risk affecting ongoing investigations.The FCA now actively removes the unutilised permissions of firms. Historically firms were expected to voluntarily request cancellation of unused permissions.The FCA permanently banned the marketing of speculative illiquid securities, including mini-bonds and loan notes, to retail investors from 1 January 2021.Anyone approached about loan notes, mini-bonds or similar high-risk investments should stop and check before investing, especially where adverts promise big, fixed returns or make the investment look simple and safe. Use the FCA’s Firm Checker and Warning List before handing over any money.

title: LIBOR/EURIBOR-related bans
raw_summary: The FCA has reviewed its regulatory action against individuals whose convictions have recently been overturned by the Court of Appeal.As these convictions formed the basis on which the FCA took its action, we have revoked the bans of Colin Bermingham, Philippe Moryoussef, Jonathan Mathew and Christian Bittar and removed the associated Final Notices from FCA channels.The FCA will take no further action against these individuals in relation to this matter.This follows our decision last year to discontinue proceedings against Tom Hayes and revoke Carlo Palombo’s ban after the Supreme Court quashed their criminal convictions.
